USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window. Keep Lists 1–3 in place as leverage, do not raise List 3 during the pause, and do not trade Meng Wanzhou or further Huawei/entity-list moves for a purchase-only deal. Press Beijing for enforceable structural commitments on forced tech transfer, IP, cyber theft, and market access, treating any soybean/energy buys as confidence-builders, not the settlement. If March 1 arrives with only vague purchase pledges, the already-announced List 3 hike remains the scheduled backstop—not a new escalation decided now.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly elevated, not existential. Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%), and China has matched with farm-heavy retaliation; soybean sales to China are down ~94–97% from a ~$12B market, storage is overflowing, and Farm Bureau/USDA data show only a token mid-December repurchase (~500k tons). That is real sectoral and political pain, but national activity is not breaking: Michigan sentiment is still 98.3, industrial production is slightly higher, and CPI is contained. The sharper US-side risk is financial: VIX at 25.58 (+47% in the window), WTI down ~31% to ~$48, the 10-year at 2.77% with a flattened curve, and a December equity slump explicitly tied to trade plus a looming Fed hike. Opportunity is also limited: the May 19 joint statement (“trade war on hold”) collapsed ten days later, so purchase promises without structural change are not a win. The Dec 1 G20 pause bought time and showed Beijing wanted the Jan 1 List 3 jump to 25% delayed, but White House and Chinese readouts already diverge (US: 90-day clock and structural reform; China: halt new tariffs and work toward eliminating them). Meng’s Dec 1 arrest and the Dec 10 Kovrig/Spavor detentions raise the odds the window blows up if we either escalate non-tariff pressure or bargain the criminal case. Lighthizer has correctly framed March 1 as a hard deadline and Meng as a separate law-enforcement track. That combination—hold existing tariffs, negotiate hard on structure, refuse both premature rollback and mid-truce escalation—matches a +0.22 threat and a 0.0 action stance.
key_factors: G20 90-day ceasefire paused the List 3 hike to 25% but left $250B of Section 301 tariffs in force
China farm retaliation has nearly shut a ~$12B soybean market (exports down ~94–97%) with only token mid-December repurchase
US real economy still intact (sentiment 98.3, IP slightly up) while markets are stressed (VIX 25.58, oil crash, flattened curve)
Meng arrest plus Kovrig/Spavor detentions risk contaminating the talks if tracks are mixed
May 2018 purchase-truce collapsed within days; Lighthizer is demanding structural IP/tech/market-access changes on a hard March 1 clock

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
VIX latest 25.58 on 2018-12-19; +8.25 / +47.6% over the window.
Michigan consumer sentiment 98.3 in December 2018 — still solid, not a demand collapse.
WTI $47.96 on 2018-12-19, down ~31% in the window.
10-year Treasury 2.77% on 2018-12-19 versus 2s at 2.63% — curve flattened amid risk-off.
White House: China to purchase a 'very substantial' amount of ag/energy/industrial goods; talks on forced tech transfer, IP, NTBs, cyber; if no deal in 90 days, 10% List 3 rises to 25%.
Lighthizer: need structural changes — open market, IP protection, stop cybertheft and forced technology transfer; March deadline treated as hard; tariffs stay until those remedies are met.
Farm Bureau: soybean exports to China down 97%; China did not immediately restart buying after G20; later state-firm orders would not close the gap.
Truce is less a breakthrough than a breakdown averted; leaders remain far apart on market access; List 1/2 25% tariffs stay until a broader agreement.
Meng arrest and trade talks were not initially the same track; mixing them would weaken the US negotiating hand on structural issues.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window to negotiate in earnest, deliver the limited purchase and auto-tariff confidence-builders already signaled after Buenos Aires, and keep structural industrial-policy red lines off the table for now. Do not add new tariffs or further hostage-style non-tariff moves that would give Washington a pretext to restore the January List-3 hike or widen coverage to the remaining export book. The aim is to freeze the tariff ceiling, buy time for exporters and domestic stimulus, and test whether a narrow goods deal can be separated from Made-in-China-2025 and entity-list demands.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already about $250B of Chinese goods (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), and the same-day Meng Wanzhou arrest on a US extradition request is firm-level targeting of Huawei after the April ZTE denial order—squarely on the CHN +0.5 anchor of export-sector hits plus champion-firm pressure. Mid-December official data showed surprisingly weak industrial production and retail sales; Q3 GDP had already slowed to 6.5%, the weakest since 2009, with unpaid factory furloughs reported in export hubs. That is a legitimacy and employment risk, not a financial-stability collapse: growth is still near the official ~6.5% target, tariffs have been partly front-run, and the Dec 1 truce suspended the scheduled Jan 1 jump of List 3 to 25%. Country-health series for China were unavailable, so the reading is deliberately milder than +0.5; a stronger dollar (+2.5% on the broad index) and US VIX at 25.6 are consistent with external pressure but are not a China FX crisis in the file. Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. Escalation would likely bring the postponed 25% rate and a threatened further ~$267B list while the domestic cycle is already softening. Full rollback or large structural concede_purchases is premature: talks only opened after the G20 dinner, US existing tariffs remain, White House and Chinese readouts still disagree on the 90-day clock and purchase quantities, and Washington is still demanding IP, tech-transfer, cyber, and industrial-policy changes China has not been willing to discuss as systemic reform. Liu He’s mid-December call and reported soybean orders plus a 40%→15% US-auto tariff cut are appropriate tactical gestures inside a negotiate stance, not a purchase-concession endgame. Canadian detentions after Meng already answered the non-tariff shock; further such steps would contaminate the trade channel Trump has already linked to the Huawei case.
key_factors: G20 90-day truce paused the Jan 1 List-3 hike from 10% to 25% but left ~$250B of Section 301 tariffs in place
Meng Wanzhou arrest (1 Dec) plus prior ZTE denial order = firm-level tech targeting; Kovrig/Spavor detentions already answered that shock
China growth is the weakest since the GFC (Q3 GDP 6.5%; mid-Dec IP and retail sales surprise to the downside; export-hub job stress)
Talks have started (Liu He–Lighthizer/Mnuchin) with only tactical goods gestures (soybeans, auto tariff 40→15) and no agreed structural package
US still threatens a March snap-back and possible coverage of remaining Chinese exports if no deal
Chinese official readouts omit the 90-day deadline and quantified purchases — room to negotiate without accepting Washington’s maximal framing
